title: Who got a pension mattered for children in one South African study
body: In the early 1990s South Africa expanded its social pension for Black residents. Esther Duflo found that pensions paid to women were associated with better growth measures for girls in their households, an effect not seen for pensions paid to men.
takeaway: Money entering a household need not be shared in the same way regardless of who receives it.
source: Esther Duflo, World Bank Economic Review (2003)
visual: an older woman and a young girl preparing a meal in a South African home

title: Girls near Bangladesh's garment jobs stayed in school longer
body: Rachel Heath and Ahmed Mushfiq Mobarak studied villages near garment factories in Bangladesh. They found that girls gained more schooling and married later when factory work became more accessible.
takeaway: Job opportunities can change how a family weighs schooling years before a girl enters the workforce.
source: Heath and Mobarak, Journal of Development Economics (2015)
visual: a girl carrying schoolbooks past a garment factory on a village road

title: A Nigerian landscape preserves ironworking alongside sacred fields
body: At Sukur, in Nigeria, a hilltop chief's palace overlooks villages and terraced fields marked with sacred symbols. Remains of iron production survive within the same landscape.
takeaway: Traces of work and belief can survive together in the layout of a community.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sukur Cultural Landscape (1999)
visual: stone field terraces below a hilltop palace amid Nigerian mountains
